title: Vector
notes:
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle law of addition. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. A scalar quantity has only magnitude.

Examples: mass, time, temperature, speed, work.

Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction. Negative vector: same magnitude, opposite direction. Null vector: zero magnitude (its direction is undefined). Unit vector: a vector of magnitude 1 along a given direction, written as $\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$. Parallel and antiparallel vectors: vectors along the same line (same or opposite sense). Position vector: vector joining the origin to a point. Collinear vectors: vectors along the same straight line.
Addition of Vectors — Triangle and Parallelogram Law
If two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ act at an angle $\theta$, the magnitude of their resultant $\vec{R} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is:

and its direction is given by $\tan\alpha = \frac{b\sin\theta}{a + b\cos\theta}$, where $\alpha$ is the angle made by the resultant with $\vec{a}$. Special cases: parallel ($\theta = 0°$) gives $R = a + b$; antiparallel ($\theta = 180°$) gives $R = |a - b|$; perpendicular ($\theta = 90°$) gives $R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Any vector $\vec{A}$ can be resolved into two perpendicular components:
with $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}$. In unit vector notation, $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$.

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$. The result is a scalar. $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$ when the vectors are perpendicular. For unit vectors: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = 0$.

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = ab\sin\theta$, directed perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors (right-hand rule). $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = 0$ when the vectors are parallel. The cross product is used for torque ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$) and angular momentum ($\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$).

summary: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Vectors are added by the triangle or parallelogram law, giving R = √(a² + b² + 2ab cos θ). A vector can be resolved into perpendicular components Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ. The dot product a·b = ab cos θ gives a scalar, while the cross product has magnitude ab sin θ and points perpendicular to both vectors.
formulas: tan α = b sin θ / (a + b cos θ)
Ax = A cos θ, Ay = A sin θ
examples: A boat crossing a river is a classic vector addition problem: the velocity of the boat relative to water added to the velocity of the river current.
Walking 3 km east then 4 km north gives a resultant displacement of 5 km north-east.

practice.question: Find the angle between two vectors of equal magnitude whose resultant has the same magnitude as either vector.
practice.answer: 120° (R² = a² + a² + 2a² cos θ = a² ⇒ cos θ = −1/2)

practice.question: Two forces of 10 N and 10 N act at 120°. Find the resultant.

keyPoints: Vectors obey the triangle law of addition; scalars do not.
A unit vector has magnitude 1 and no unit.
The resultant of two perpendicular vectors is √(a² + b²).
The dot product of perpendicular vectors is zero.
The cross product of parallel vectors is zero.
Torque and angular momentum are expressed with cross products.
